catalog_quote: The phoneme inventory of Bit is introduced in Table 1 below (Badenoch 2015). Bit has 10 simple vowels, all contrasting for length, and four diphthongs. [...] The consonant system includes 21 phonemes (Table 2), all of which can occur in word and syllable initial position. With the exception of the voiced stop series, all occur as coda as well. [...] Bit is a disyllabic, iambic language, with many onset clusters and a rich system of morphology. [p. 8:] ... this morpheme is limited to /CrC/ position in a minor syllable ... [p. 12, on Bumang/Khang:] ... reducing the older disyllabic structure to a mostly monosyllabic one, reducing onset clusters and developing tones in the process.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19 pp., text layer; Kobe CUFS repository record 2369 confirms Annals of Foreign Studies 92: 5-23, 2016, file). PDF page 2 = journal p. 6 (paper runs pp. 5-23). Both quoted sentences are there verbatim: "The phoneme inventory of Bit is introduced in Table 1 below (Badenoch 2015). Bit has 10 simple vowels, all contrasting for length, and four diphthongs." (before Table 1) and, immediately after Table 2 'Bit consonants', "Bit is a disyllabic, iambic language, with many onset clusters and a rich system of morphology." The [..] in the report correctly elides Table 1, the consonant paragraph and Table 2. Surrounding text supports the reading: p. 7 says the plural /r/ "is limited to /CrC/…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bit words are mono- or sesquisyllabic ('disyllabic' in Badenoch's usage: a minor syllable plus a major syllable) and iambic, i.e. prominence falls on the final (major) syllable; the language is atonal. This matches the second-hand summary in Sidwell 2015: 55 (via Wikipedia): 'Stress falls on the final syllable', template (C1(ə(C2))).ˈCi(Cm)V(ː)(Cf).
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; compounding and expressive formations can yield true disyllables (per Sidwell 2015 summary), with no statement on their stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical items in citation form and text data from Ban Bompiang, Luang Namtha, Laos, 2011-2015). The statement is a one-line typological characterisation ('iambic'), not an explicit stress rule; the fuller sketch is the unpublished Badenoch 2015 SEALS 25 paper as summarised in Sidwell 2015: 55-57.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Bit of Ban Bompiang, Luang Namtha, Laos (Badenoch's fieldwork 2011-2015); Badenoch treats Chinese Buxing (Gao 2004; Mengla, Yunnan) as a closely related dialect of the same language, so it applies to bitt1240 as a whole. Two of the four Glottolog 5.1 references for bitt1240 (Tạ 2021, Tạ 2023) actually describe Kháng of Vietnam (ISO kjm, Glottolog khan1274), a tonal sister language in the same Khao subgroup — not Bit; our earlier survey's note '(= Bit [bgk] variety)' is wrong on that point.
